scenario: AITA for not wanting to share an animal crossing town with my girlfriend? | This is kind of petty but here goes. The new animal crossing game is coming out and you can only have one village per nintendo switch console. my girlfriend and I both have a switch, but she wants to share one village with me so were both using one switch to play. I told her I would rather us both get the game so we can play online and customize our towns the way we want to, but she disagreed. I even told her I would buy her the game but she said she wants to feel a sense of "togetherness" in animal crossing which I just dont get. When I insisted we play on different consoles, even with valid reasoning and all that, she stormed out. called me an asshole baby, and told me to grow up. Animal crossing is a beloved series for me and I want to be able to make my village the way I want to, and I would also like to be able to play with my girlfriend online. AITA?

The user prefers each to have their own game and play online separately, customizing their own towns. He offered to buy her the game, but she wants "togetherness" through sharing the same village. When he insisted on separate consoles, she got upset, called him an asshole, etc.

Hmm. Moral acceptability here probably depends on whether his choice respects both parties' autonomy and reasonable expectations. Let's break it down.

In relationships, especially around hobbies or personal interests, it's common for people to have different preferences. Animal Crossing is a game where players often enjoy personal customization. Each player might want their own town to design freely without compromise. Sharing a single village would mean both have to agree on every aspect, which could lead to conflicts or one person feeling their preferences aren't respected.

The user offered to buy her the game so they can each have their own. That seems fair. He's not refusing to play together; he's suggesting playing online separately, which still allows interaction but with individual control. The girlfriend's desire for "togetherness" through sharing a village might be her way of bonding, but forcing someone to share a single save file when they have separate consoles could be seen as imposing her preference without considering his.

But wait, the key here is whether his refusal is unreasonable. If they both own consoles, there's no technical reason they can't each have their own game. Sharing a village on one console would require them to both use that same console, which might not be practical if they want to play at different times or have their own progress. But the girlfriend wants to share the same village, which would mean they're both playing on the same save file. However, in Animal Crossing, typically each console has its own save file, and you can't have two people playing the same village on different consoles unless they're using the same console. Wait, actually, in Animal Crossing: New Horizons, each console has its own island. So if they have separate consoles, each has their own island. To play together online, they can visit each other's islands. But if they want to share the same island, they'd have to both play on the same console, which might mean taking turns or playing together on one device. But the user's point is that he wants each to have their own console and game so they can customize their own towns and play online. That's standard for the game. 

So the girlfriend's request to share one village on one console would mean they both have to use that one console, which might not be ideal. For example, if she wants to play on her own console, but he wants to use his, but she's insisting they use one console for the same village. But if they each have their own console, they can each have their own island and play together online. So the user's preference is actually the normal way to play. Sharing a village on one console would mean they're both on the same island, which might not be what the user wants. 

So the user's stance is reasonable. He's not being unreasonable by wanting his own island. In fact, the game is designed for each player to have their own island when using separate consoles. Sharing a single island would require them to both use the same console, which might not be practical. So his request to each have their own game and play online is standard and reasonable. 

The girlfriend's desire for "togetherness" through sharing a village might be her way of wanting to spend time together, but forcing him to give up his own island (since if they share one console, he'd have to use her console, but he has his own) — but actually, if they share one console, they'd both be playing on the same island, which might not be what he wants. But he has his own console, so he could just buy the game for his own and play separately. 

So the issue here is whether it's morally acceptable for him to prefer separate islands. Since the game allows for that, and it's a personal choice, his preference is valid. He's not being unreasonable. The girlfriend might feel that sharing the same island creates more togetherness, but that's her preference. However, expecting him to compromise his own enjoyment of the game by forcing him to share a single island when he has his own console might not be fair. 

In moral terms, respecting each other's autonomy in personal hobbies is important. If he wants to have his own island to customize as he likes, that's his right. The fact that he offered to buy her the game shows he's willing to support her playing, but on her own terms. Her reaction of calling him an asshole might be overreacting, but the question is about his action. 

So his action of not wanting to share the same village (i.e., preferring separate islands) is morally acceptable. Because it's his choice how to engage with his hobby, and he's not being unreasonable. The game's design supports separate islands, so he's not being petty; he's just wanting to play the game as intended for multiple players with separate consoles. 

Therefore, the answer should be 1. It's morally acceptable.
